Introduction

An AI coding agent is a program that runs on your computer and can do everything you allow it to — read and edit files, run commands in the terminal, install packages, create branches, write tests, deploy software. You describe what you want in plain language and it works autonomously until the job is done. It is not a chatbot you copy answers from. It acts.

There are many coding agents available. This course covers some of the most widely used ones: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor and Windsurf. Select your agent above — the install steps differ per agent, but from Session 2 onwards everything is the same. If you use a different agent not listed here, the install steps in this session will look different, but the rest of the course still applies.

Installing Node.js

Claude Code requires Node.js to run. Go to nodejs.org/en/download and choose the LTS version.

nodejs.org/en/download — select the LTS version

Click the green Windows Installer (.msi) button to download, then run it and click Next on every screen.

Click "Windows Installer (.msi)" to download the installer

When the installer finishes, open a terminal: press Win + X → choose Terminal or PowerShell. Then verify:

node --version

Click macOS Installer (.pkg) to download, run it and follow the steps. Then open a terminal (press Cmd + Space, type Terminal, press Enter) and verify:

node --version

Open a terminal (Ctrl + Alt + T) and run:

curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_lts.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt-get install -y nodejs
node --version

For Fedora / RHEL: sudo dnf install nodejs

You should see something like v20.11.0. If you get an error, close the terminal and open it again.

Installing Claude Code

1 · Get access

The easiest way is a Claude Max or Pro subscription at claude.ai — this covers Claude Code usage without a separate API key.

Alternatively, create an API key at console.anthropic.com → API Keys → Create Key.

2 · Install

npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

3 · Run it

Navigate to your project folder in the terminal, then:

claude

First run: it opens a browser to log in with your Claude account. If you use an API key instead, paste it when prompted.

Verify it works

Try: "What files are in this folder?"

Installing Codex

1 · Get your API key

Go to platform.openai.com/api-keys → Create new secret key. Copy it.

2 · Install

npm install -g @openai/codex

3 · Set your API key

[System.Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('OPENAI_API_KEY','sk-your-key-here','User')

Close and reopen your terminal after running this.

echo 'export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-your-key-here"' >> ~/.zshrc && source ~/.zshrc
echo 'export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-your-key-here"' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc

4 · Run it

codex

Verify it works

Try: "What files are in this folder?"

Installing Cursor

1 · Download and install

Go to cursor.com → click Download for Windows → run the installer.

Go to cursor.com → click Download for Mac → open the .dmg and drag Cursor to Applications.

Go to cursor.com → download the .AppImage → open a terminal and run:

chmod +x cursor-*.AppImage && ./cursor-*.AppImage

2 · Get access

On first launch, sign up at cursor.com. The free tier includes limited AI usage. A Pro subscription gives unlimited access including Claude and GPT-4o models.

Alternatively go to Cursor Settings → Models and add your own API key from Anthropic or OpenAI.

3 · Open your project

File → Open Folder → choose your project directory.

4 · Start the Agent

Press Ctrl+Shift+I (Windows / Linux) or Cmd+Shift+I (Mac) to open Composer. Switch the mode to Agent in the top-right of the Composer panel.

Verify it works

Try: "What files are in this folder?"

Installing Windsurf

1 · Download and install

Go to codeium.com/windsurf → click Download for Windows → run the installer.

Go to codeium.com/windsurf → click Download for Mac → open the .dmg and drag Windsurf to Applications.

Go to codeium.com/windsurf → download the .tar.gz → open a terminal, extract and run:

tar -xzf windsurf-*.tar.gz && ./windsurf

2 · Get access

Sign up at codeium.com — Windsurf has a generous free tier. Sign in on first launch.

3 · Open your project

File → Open Folder → choose your project directory.

4 · Start Cascade

Open Cascade from the sidebar or press Ctrl+L (Windows / Linux) or Cmd+L (Mac). Set the mode to Write for full agent capabilities.

Verify it works

Try: "What files are in this folder?"

Introduction

Your agent needs a home — a dedicated folder it treats as its own. This session creates that folder, gives the agent a written set of rules to follow, and ends with the agent creating its own startup script. From then on a double-click is all it takes to open a fresh session in your workspace.

Quick Start

If you want to skip the manual steps, download the Jengo starter workspace — it includes a ready-made bootstrap file, rules, and startup scripts for all supported agents.

Download Jengo workspace starter (zip)

Extract the zip into your project folder, then continue from the Bootstrap prompt step below.

Create Workspace Directory

Open Cursor → File → Open Folder → create a new folder and open it.

Open Windsurf → File → Open Folder → create a new folder and open it.

mkdir my-project
cd my-project
mkdir my-project && cd my-project
mkdir my-project
cd my-project
mkdir my-project && cd my-project
mkdir my-project
cd my-project
mkdir my-project && cd my-project

Create Bootstrap File

The bootstrap file tells the agent who it is, what this project is, and what it is allowed to do — automatically, every session. Create it in the project root:

Filename: CLAUDE.md

# My Project

## What this is
[Describe your project in 1-2 sentences]

## Rules
- Never commit directly to main
- Always create a pull request
- Ask before deleting any file

## What you can do without asking
- Read, edit and create files
- Run tests and builds
- Install packages
- Create branches and commits

## Commands
- Test:           npm test
- Build:          npm run build
- Deploy staging: ./deploy.sh staging

Enable auto-approve

Run Claude Code with the skip-permissions flag so it works without stopping to ask:

claude --dangerously-skip-permissions

To make this permanent, add to ~/.claude/settings.json:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(*)", "Edit(*)", "Write(*)", "Read(*)"]
  }
}

Bootstrap prompt

Start the agent and paste this as your very first message. It reads the bootstrap file, confirms the rules, and creates a startup script so future sessions start with a double-click:

Read CLAUDE.md. Summarise the project in one sentence and confirm the 3 most important rules you will follow. Then create a startup script in this folder:
- Windows: start.bat — navigates to this directory and runs: claude --dangerously-skip-permissions
- Mac / Linux: start.sh — same, then run: chmod +x start.sh

The agent will create a script that looks like this:

@echo off
cd /d "%~dp0"
claude --dangerously-skip-permissions
#!/bin/bash
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
claude --dangerously-skip-permissions

Introduction

Git records every change your agent makes as a named snapshot. If something breaks you can see exactly what changed and roll it back. GitHub stores your project in the cloud — a backup, and the place where multiple agents or team members can collaborate without overwriting each other. This session installs Git, initializes your project, creates a GitHub repository, and connects the two.

Installing Git

Go to git-scm.com — click Download for Windows — run the installer — leave all settings on default. Then open a new terminal.

Open a terminal and run:

git --version

If Git is not installed, macOS will prompt you to install the Command Line Tools — click Install.

sudo apt install git

For Fedora / RHEL: sudo dnf install git

Verify:

git --version

Initialize your project:

git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"

Connecting to GitHub

Go to github.com — sign up or log in — click the + in the top right — New repository.

  • Give it a name (e.g. my-project) and set it to Private
  • Leave everything else on default — do not add a README or .gitignore (you already have files locally)
  • Click Create repository

Copy your repository URL (e.g. https://github.com/your-username/my-project.git), then in your terminal:

git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/my-project.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

After every agent session, commit and push the changes:

git add .
git commit -m "What the agent did"
git push

Introduction

A task manager gives your agent a shared understanding of what needs to be done, what is in progress, and what is waiting for your review. Without one, you have to describe the context every session. With one, the agent can read the backlog itself, pick up where it left off, move tasks to done, and flag blockers — without you having to repeat yourself.

It also gives you visibility. You see every task the agent created or updated, which means you stay in control without being in the loop for every small step.

Connect Your Task Manager

.tm-sel{display:flex;gap:8px;margin:18px 0 24px;flex-wrap:wrap;} .tm-btn{font-family:'Sora',sans-serif;font-size:13px;font-weight:600;padding:8px 18px;border-radius:999px;border:1.5px solid var(--line);background:#fff;color:var(--muted);cursor:pointer;transition:all .15s;} .tm-btn.active{background:var(--green-700);color:#fff;border-color:var(--green-700);} .tm-section{display:none;} .tm-section.tm-active{display:block;}

ClickUp offers a built-in MCP server. Go to app.clickup.com → Settings → Integrations → Claude MCP to generate your connection details.

Add the MCP server to your agent's settings file. For Claude Code, open ~/.claude/settings.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "clickup": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.clickup.com",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer your-api-token-here" }
    }
  }
}

Get your API token at app.clickup.com → Settings → Apps → API Token.

Test it — start your agent and ask:

What tasks are currently in my backlog?

The agent should list your open tasks. Now add this to your bootstrap file so the agent uses ClickUp every session:

## Task manager (ClickUp)
- Always check the task board at the start of a session
- Update task status when you start and finish work
- If you create a subtask, link it to the parent task

Jira supports MCP via Atlassian's Remote MCP Server (available in Jira Software cloud). Go to your-site.atlassian.net → Settings → Apps → Atlassian MCP to enable it and get your connection URL.

Add the MCP server to your agent's settings file. For Claude Code, open ~/.claude/settings.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "jira": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer your-api-token-here" }
    }
  }
}

Get your API token at id.atlassian.com → Security → API tokens → Create API token.

Test it — start your agent and ask:

What issues are currently assigned to me?

The agent should list your open Jira issues. Now add this to your bootstrap file so the agent uses Jira every session:

## Task manager (Jira)
- Always check Jira at the start of a session
- Update issue status when you start and finish work
- Add a comment to the issue when you make significant progress
(function(){ var btns = document.querySelectorAll('.tm-btn'); var sects = document.querySelectorAll('.tm-section'); var active = localStorage.getItem('jl-tm') || 'clickup'; function setTm(key) { active = key; try { localStorage.setItem('jl-tm', key); } catch(e){} sects.forEach(function(s){ s.classList.toggle('tm-active', s.getAttribute('data-tm') === key); }); btns.forEach(function(b){ b.classList.toggle('active', b.getAttribute('data-tm') === key); }); } btns.forEach(function(b){ b.addEventListener('click', function(){ setTm(b.getAttribute('data-tm')); }); }); setTm(active); })();

Parallel Agents with Git Worktrees

Two agents working in the same folder will overwrite each other. Git worktrees give each agent its own directory — same repository, no conflicts.

git worktree add ../my-project-feature feature/my-feature

One agent per directory. When the feature is done:

git worktree remove ../my-project-feature

Automating Deployment

Create a deploy script and give the agent permission to run it.

#!/bin/bash
set -e
ssh user@your-server "cd /var/www/mysite && git pull && npm run build"
echo "Deployed."

Add to your bootstrap file:

## Deployment
- After finishing a task: ./deploy.sh staging
- Production: never without my approval

AI Code Review

Before every pull request, have the agent check its own work:

Review the changes you just made. Look for bugs and anything that does not match our standards. Fix what you find. Then create a pull request.

Or add it to your bootstrap file so it runs automatically:

## Before every pull request
1. Run npm test -- fix any failures
2. Run npm run lint -- fix warnings
3. Then create the PR

Control from Your Phone

Install Claude (or ChatGPT) on your phone. Connect it to the same task board via MCP. From your phone:

  • "Add a task: the contact form sends to the wrong address"
  • "What is being worked on right now?"
  • "Staging looks good — deploy to production"

Your phone is the command interface for your entire development system.

The Full Lifecycle

  1. You spot a bug on your phone — tell the AI
  2. Agent creates a task, finds the issue, writes the fix, deploys to staging
  3. You check staging: "Looks good"
  4. Agent deploys to production

No code editor. No terminal. Just conversations.
